extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two conformity-assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: an internal-control procedure based on Annex VI, and a procedure based on assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation involving a notified body based on Annex VII.

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric identification/categorisation), the provider may choose internal control or a notified-body assessment, with the choice affected by whether harmonised standards or common specifications under Articles 40–41 were applied.

For high-risk AI systems covered by existing EU sectoral legislation listed in Annex I, Section A (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies verifying compliance with the AI-specific requirements.

Annex VII (notified-body) assessment is mandatory for biometric identification systems and certain critical-infrastructure AI systems; most other high-risk AI systems may use the Annex VI self-assessment route.

Under Article 43, a provider may choose any notified body for the Annex VII procedure, except that where the high-risk AI system is to be put into service by law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities, or by EU institutions, bodies, offices or agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body.

A high-risk AI system that is substantially modified after its initial conformity assessment must undergo a new conformity assessment, unless the modification was predetermined by the provider at the time of the initial assessment and the system continues to learn within that predetermined scope.

Article 46 permits a market surveillance authority, by way of derogation from Article 43 and upon a duly justified request, to authorise the placing on the market or putting into service of a specific high-risk AI system for a limited period, for exceptional reasons of public security, protection of life and health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets.

Under Annex VII, point 4.5, where necessary and after all other reasonable means have been exhausted, a notified body may be granted access to the training and trained models of the AI system, including relevant parameters, subject to existing EU law on intellectual property and confidentiality.

Section 5 of the AI Act (Articles 40–51) covers harmonised standards, common specifications, presumption of conformity, conformity assessment, certificates, notified-body information obligations, derogations, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking and registration.
The Commission may adopt delegated acts under Article 43(5) to update Annex VI (internal control) and Annex VII (QMS/technical documentation assessment) procedures in light of technical progress.

As of March 2026, the notified-body ecosystem for AI Act conformity assessments was still being built, with designation processes ongoing across Member States and capacity described as limited, ahead of the (non-moving) August 2026 deadline.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act for medical-device-related high-risk AI systems, despite the MDR/IVDR data cited running to 31 October 2025.

High-risk AI obligations under the EU AI Act are described as fully applying from 2 August 2026, after which conformity assessment (including notified-body routes where applicable) and CE marking/declaration-of-conformity obligations become mandatory.
As of October 2025, the Commission's NANDO database listed 51 MDR-designated notified bodies and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies (sectoral medical-device regime, not AI-Act-specific designations).

A Commission proposal, COM(2025) 836, would amend the AI Act to add a new Annex XIV listing codes and categories of AI systems for the Commission's NANDO information system, to support notified-body designation scope, and would also amend Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 for smoother integration of AI Act high-risk requirements.

A Council document (ST-7322-2026) sets out a list of draft codes and categories of AI systems under Annex I of the AI Act, intended to define the scope of designation of conformity assessment bodies notified under the relevant Article.

Under the separate EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), as of late June 2026 zero notified bodies had been designated in the Commission's NANDO database, despite the CRA's notified-body rules having started to apply on 11 June 2026, with a target of 11 December 2026 for sufficient notified-body capacity and full application from 11 December 2027.

Notified bodies must comply with information obligations toward notifying authorities (Article 45) and are listed with identification numbers under Article 35, which some sources describe as establishing the administrative and listing framework for notified bodies under the AI Act.

open_issues: None of the sources confirm that any notified bodies have yet been formally designated specifically under the EU AI Act as of a date close to October 2026; the most recent dated sources (March–April 2026) indicate none or an ongoing, incomplete designation process, leaving the current (October 2026) status unconfirmed.

It is unclear whether COM(2025) 836 (the proposed new Annex XIV / NANDO amendment) and the related Council document ST-7322-2026 code/category list have been formally adopted or remain in the legislative proposal stage as of October 2026.

The sources do not clarify how many of the existing MDR (51) and IVDR (19) notified bodies have obtained, or are expected to obtain, separate or extended AI Act designation, nor the timeline for such dual designation.

The relationship and potential overlap between notified bodies designated under the Cyber Resilience Act and those designated under the AI Act is not addressed by the sources, risking confusion between the two separate regimes.

Earlier proposal-stage texts of Article 43 (2021 and November 2022 drafts) are not clearly reconciled with the final adopted text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 in the sources, leaving open which specific procedural details changed between proposal and final law.

The exact scope and criteria market surveillance authorities use when acting as notified bodies for law-enforcement, immigration, asylum or EU-institution systems (per Article 43) are not detailed in the sources.

The practical consequences for providers if no notified body is available/designated by the August 2026 deadline (e.g., for Annex VII-mandatory systems such as biometric identification) are not addressed.
report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act and the Status of Notified Body Designation

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two main routes for demonstrating conformity of high-risk AI systems: internal control (Annex VI) and third-party assessment by a notified body of the quality management system and technical documentation (Annex VII), with the applicable route depending on the system's category and the use of harmonised standards ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [powerquant.eu](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment)). Despite obligations becoming fully applicable on 2 August 2026, available evidence through early-to-mid 2026 indicates that no notified bodies had yet been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, leaving significant uncertainty about operational readiness ([eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Routes
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two conformity-assessment pathways for high-risk AI systems: an internal-control procedure under Annex VI, and a notified-body-based assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation under Annex VII (low confidence) ([powerquant.eu](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [fpf.org](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For systems listed under Annex III, point 1 (biometric identification/categorisation), providers may generally choose between internal control or notified-body assessment, with the choice affected by whether harmonised standards or common specifications were applied (low confidence) ([futurium.ec.europa.eu](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). Some sources further suggest Annex VII assessment is mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical-infrastructure systems, while most other high-risk systems may rely on self-assessment (low confidence) ([quantamixsolutions.com](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU sectoral legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery under Annex I, Section A), providers must follow that sectoral legislation's conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [vde.com](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

### Procedural Details
Providers may generally select any notified body for Annex VII assessment, except where systems are intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority performs the notified-body function (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Substantially modified high-risk systems require a new conformity assessment unless the modification was predetermined and falls within the system's continued-learning scope (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard conformity assessment and authorise temporary market placement for exceptional public-security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Under Annex VII, point 4.5, notified bodies may, as a last resort, obtain access to training data and trained models, subject to IP and confidentiality law (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). The Commission may update Annexes VI and VII via delegated acts to reflect technical progress (low confidence) ([fpf.org](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
As of October 2025, the Commission's NANDO database listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies under the separate medical devices regime, not AI-Act-specific designations (high confidence) ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). As of March 2026, the AI-Act-specific notified-body ecosystem was still being built, with designation ongoing and capacity described as limited ahead of the August 2026 deadline (low confidence) ([eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act for medical-device-related high-risk AI systems (low confidence) ([aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). A Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would add a new Annex XIV listing codes/categories of AI systems to support NANDO-based designation scope (medium confidence) ([data.consilium.europa.eu](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)), and a related Council document (ST-7322-2026) lists draft codes/categories to define designation scope (medium confidence) ([data.consilium.europa.eu](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
No direct contradictions were detected, but several claims carry low confidence (below 0.4) due to thin sourcing or lack of dates, including the Annex VI/VII route description, the mandatory-Annex-VII-for-biometric claim, delegated act provisions, and all timeline-related claims about notified body designation status. The 2021 and 2022 proposal-stage texts of Article 43 are not clearly reconciled with the final adopted Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear whether any notified bodies have been formally designated under the AI Act as of October 2026, or whether COM(2025) 836 and ST-7322-2026 have been adopted. The relationship between existing MDR/IVDR notified bodies and AI Act designation, the criteria for market surveillance authorities acting as notified bodies, and consequences of insufficient notified-body capacity by the August 2026 deadline all require further research.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act and the Status of Notified Body Designation

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two main routes for demonstrating conformity of high-risk AI systems: internal control (Annex VI) and third-party assessment by a notified body of the quality management system and technical documentation (Annex VII), with the applicable route depending on the system's category and the use of harmonised standards ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [powerquant.eu](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment)). Despite obligations becoming fully applicable on 2 August 2026, available evidence through early-to-mid 2026 indicates that no notified bodies had yet been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, leaving significant uncertainty about operational readiness ([eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Routes
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two conformity-assessment pathways for high-risk AI systems: an internal-control procedure under Annex VI, and a notified-body-based assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation under Annex VII (low confidence) ([powerquant.eu](https://powerquant.eu/en/ai-act-conformity-assessment), [fpf.org](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For systems listed under Annex III, point 1 (biometric identification/categorisation), providers may generally choose between internal control or notified-body assessment, with the choice affected by whether harmonised standards or common specifications were applied (low confidence) ([futurium.ec.europa.eu](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). Some sources further suggest Annex VII assessment is mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical-infrastructure systems, while most other high-risk systems may rely on self-assessment (low confidence) ([quantamixsolutions.com](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU sectoral legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery under Annex I, Section A), providers must follow that sectoral legislation's conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [vde.com](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)).

### Procedural Details
Providers may generally select any notified body for Annex VII assessment, except where systems are intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority performs the notified-body function (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Substantially modified high-risk systems require a new conformity assessment unless the modification was predetermined and falls within the system's continued-learning scope (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard conformity assessment and authorise temporary market placement for exceptional public-security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Under Annex VII, point 4.5, notified bodies may, as a last resort, obtain access to training data and trained models, subject to IP and confidentiality law (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). The Commission may update Annexes VI and VII via delegated acts to reflect technical progress (low confidence) ([fpf.org](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
As of October 2025, the Commission's NANDO database listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies under the separate medical devices regime, not AI-Act-specific designations (high confidence) ([eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). As of March 2026, the AI-Act-specific notified-body ecosystem was still being built, with designation ongoing and capacity described as limited ahead of the August 2026 deadline (low confidence) ([eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act for medical-device-related high-risk AI systems (low confidence) ([aiact-navigator.com](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). A Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would add a new Annex XIV listing codes/categories of AI systems to support NANDO-based designation scope (medium confidence) ([data.consilium.europa.eu](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)), and a related Council document (ST-7322-2026) lists draft codes/categories to define designation scope (medium confidence) ([data.consilium.europa.eu](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
No direct contradictions were detected, but several claims carry low confidence (below 0.4) due to thin sourcing or lack of dates, including the Annex VI/VII route description, the mandatory-Annex-VII-for-biometric claim, delegated act provisions, and all timeline-related claims about notified body designation status. The 2021 and 2022 proposal-stage texts of Article 43 are not clearly reconciled with the final adopted Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear whether any notified bodies have been formally designated under the AI Act as of October 2026, or whether COM(2025) 836 and ST-7322-2026 have been adopted. The relationship between existing MDR/IVDR notified bodies and AI Act designation, the criteria for market surveillance authorities acting as notified bodies, and consequences of insufficient notified-body capacity by the August 2026 deadline all require further research.
